title: A Hotpot Night
summary: A weekend hotpot at home got me thinking about friendships built around the kids — from a chance meeting while walking downstairs last year, to camping, swimming, birthdays, and now late nights over hotpot and a drink.
markdown:
![image]()

Last weekend we had one of the other families over for hotpot.

"Had over" makes it sound formal. It wasn't. The other dad mentioned they were doing hotpot that night; my wife jumped in immediately — then just come eat with us. That's parent socializing in a nutshell: short decision cycle, fast execution, very little ceremony. If the kids are happy together, the adults don't have to sit there scrolling either.

My mom rushed to the wet market. Vegetables, tofu skin — but no beef. Market beef always seems to vanish exactly when you need it; some local branch of Murphy's Law. So the job fell to me: beef rolls from Freshippo NB (Hema NB).

The store was packed. I'd heard Freshippo was struggling, stores closing, looking terminal. Then they launched Freshippo NB — a name that still feels slightly self-conscious to me — and business came roaring back. I was picking beef rolls at the cold case while an older man next to me studied the lamb price tags, muttering, "this one's expensive, that one's expensive, all of it expensive." I felt for him. Still put two boxes of beef in the cart.

Passing the seafood section I remembered my wife likes salmon and grabbed a box. In moments like that you get a brief, flattering illusion that you're a good husband — for the low price of a few dozen yuan.

At the drinks aisle: a craft beer with Longjing tea flavor. Abstract concept. I tried to imagine green tea and beer in the same mouthful, failed, and texted the other dad: "small drink?" Instant reply: "sure." Two cans it was.

## Hotpot bubbling

The pot bubbled and steamed.

The kids played in the living room, darting over for a bite, then back to the toys. The adults stayed at the table — parenting tips to work stories, recent news to small frustrations.

We don't work in the same field, and somehow it never felt forced. One topic into the next, laughter in waves. A little alcohol helped — that Longjing craft beer did have a hint of tea, but it was still mostly beer — and the conversation opened up.

At some point we were talking about school plans for the kids and realized it was already past eleven.

"If the kids didn't have school tomorrow, we could keep going," he said on the way out.

I agreed completely.

## How we got here

We've known each other a little over a year.

One weekend afternoon last year I was downstairs with my kid. He ran over to another kid; they clicked immediately. The other parent and I drifted into conversation the usual way — how old, which kindergarten, where do you go on weekends, the small frictions of raising kids.

I didn't imagine that accidental meeting would turn into something this easy.

Later we camped together, swam, celebrated birthdays. Every time the kids had a blast, and the adults got more comfortable. From "chat a bit while the kids play" to talking about family, work, life — the shift felt natural. No performance, no awkward distance.

## On making friends

Growing up in the village, basically everyone knew everyone. How many people in each house, how old the kids were, whose family had good news — common knowledge. Making friends was automatic. Step outside and you ran into people; a few sentences and you were already mid-conversation.

Now? After work I don't even know the people on my floor. Elevator encounters: a nod, a "hi," then back behind closed doors.

Sometimes I wonder if we just stopped wanting friends.

I don't think that's it. Without the kids, I probably wouldn't have gone out of my way to meet anyone new either. Not because I don't want to — more because there's no natural opening, no reason. Everyone's busy. Everyone has a life. Forced socializing doesn't feel necessary.

And yet. Sitting at that hotpot table, laughing easily, I could feel that people still need this. Talking, laughing, raising kids in parallel, trading the small pieces of daily life — that's not optional noise. That's the thing.

Modern life strips away a lot of the old automatic social scenes. Kids, at least, hand some of that back.

## After

Writing this, I'm back at that table: pot bubbling, kids laughing, adults who couldn't stop talking.

It felt good. Really good.

Thanks to the kids for the introductions. Thanks to these friends for making the parenting road less lonely.

And for the record: that Longjing craft beer did have a little tea in it.
